## Chapter 39: Retirement Announcement

BA planned October retirement (end of summer schedule) while Air France chose May. BA switched its Forum 150 announcement from April 9, 2003—34th anniversary of Concorde's first flight—to April 10. Bannister, in uniform, delivered the news to senior management, hitting the "Marmite factor": roughly two-thirds expressed sadness, the remainder relief, with no ambivalence. He became company spokesman, coining the line universally adopted: "It's the right decision at the right time for the right reasons."

On Branson's offer, a senior Virgin pilot told Bannister: "Thank God… because it would probably send us bust!" Retaining one aircraft for air shows required a Certificate of Airworthiness and Type Certificate—far higher standards than a "Permit to Fly." Infrastructure costs of £60 million per annum would have risen by another £40 million and didn't shrink with fleet reduction: even one aircraft would cost "a million a week." Airbus, focused on the A380 and A320, had no interest in retaining the Type Certificate, partly because air-intake computer technology remained proprietary and secret for military aircraft.

Public discussion shifted to celebrating Concorde's legacy. Edward de Bono observed she appealed to "both sides of the brain"—analytical and artistic. For Bannister, most Brits had "individually come to feel a sense of ownership. That's my Concorde up there."

## Chapter 39: Retirement Announcement

The retirement timing differed between airlines: BA planned October (end of summer schedule), while Air France chose May. BA switched its Forum 150 announcement from April 9, 2003—anniversary of Concorde's first flight, 34 years earlier—to April 10. Bannister, in uniform, delivered the news to senior management, hitting what he called the "Marmite factor": roughly two-thirds expressed sadness, the remainder relief, with no ambivalence. He became company spokesman, coining the line that became universally adopted: "It's the right decision at the right time for the right reasons."

Regarding Richard Branson's offer to take the fleet, a senior Virgin pilot told Bannister: "You’re not really going to give Concorde to us, are you, Mike?" When Bannister replied "not a chance in hell," the pilot said "Thank God… because it would probably send us bust!"

On retaining one aircraft for air shows, the answer lay in certification. Concorde required a Certificate of Airworthiness and Type Certificate—far higher standards than a "Permit to Fly." Infrastructure costs of £60 million per annum would have risen by another £40 million and didn't shrink with fleet reduction: even reduced to one aircraft, the cost would be "a million a week." Airbus, focused on the A380 and A320, had no interest in retaining the Type Certificate, partly because the air-intake computer technology remained proprietary and secret for military aircraft applications.

As spring turned to summer, public discussion shifted to celebration of Concorde's legacy. Edward de Bono observed she appealed to "both sides of the brain"—analytical and artistic. For Bannister, the simpler truth: most Brits had "individually come to feel a sense of ownership. That's my Concorde up there."

He became company spokesman, coining the line universally adopted: "It's the right decision at the right time for the right reasons."


Bannister fielded questions about the decision. When asked about Branson's offer, he recalled a senior Virgin pilot's reaction: "Thank God… because it would probably send us bust!" The issue with retaining one aircraft for air shows centered on certification—Concorde required a Certificate of Airworthiness and Type Certificate, far stricter than a "Permit to Fly."
